dryRun.title: ES Modules vs CommonJS
dryRun.note: ESM imports are analysed before the code runs, so bundlers can drop unused code. An imported binding is live: if the module changes it, you see the new value. Every module runs once and is cached; later imports get the same instance.

think.q: import('data:text/javascript,export let n = 1; export function inc() { n++ }').then((m) => { m.inc(); console.log(m.n) })
why: ESM exports are live bindings, so the importer sees n change to 2. In CommonJS you would get a copy of the old value.
think.exec: import('data:text/javascript,export let n = 1; export function inc() { n++ }').then((m) => { m.inc(); console.log(m.n) })

think.q: import('data:text/javascript,export const o = { hits: 0 }').then(async (m1) => { m1.o.hits++; const m2 = await import('data:text/javascript,export const o = { hits: 0 }'); console.log(m2.o.hits, m1 === m2) })
why: A module is evaluated once per URL and cached; importing the same specifier again returns the same module instance (and the same object).
think.exec: import('data:text/javascript,export const o = { hits: 0 }').then(async (m1) => { m1.o.hits++; const m2 = await import('data:text/javascript,export const o = { hits: 0 }'); console.log(m2.o.hits, m1 === m2) })

think.q: import('data:text/javascript,export default 1; export const two = 2').then((m) => console.log(Object.keys(m).sort().join()))
why: A namespace object holds the named exports plus default.

think.q: Why can import() (dynamic import) make an app load faster?
opts: It splits code: the module is fetched only when that line runs
why: Load rarely used routes and heavy libraries on demand.

think.q: In Node, a file with "type": "module" in package.json uses require("./x"). What happens?
opts: require is not defined in ES modules: use import (or createRequire)
why: ESM and CJS have different loaders; mixing them needs care.

try.task: Build a tiny module system: createRegistry() returns { define(name, factory), require(name) }. factory(require, exports) fills exports. Each module runs once; later requires return the cached exports. Requiring an unknown name throws.
examples: const r = createRegistry(); r.define("a", (req, ex) => { ex.v = 1 }); r.require("a").v  // 1
// factory runs only on the first require
try.hint: Keep two Maps: factories and cache. Put the exports object in the cache BEFORE running the factory (that is how cycles work in CommonJS).

checks.verify: const r = createRegistry(); r.define("a", (req, ex) => { ex.v = 1 }); assert(r.require("a").v === 1, "exports")

checks.t: a module runs once and is cached
checks.verify: let runs = 0; const r = createRegistry(); r.define("a", (req, ex) => { runs++; ex.o = {} }); assert(r.require("a").o === r.require("a").o && runs === 1, "cache")

checks.t: modules can require each other, unknown names throw
checks.verify: const r = createRegistry(); r.define("b", (req, ex) => { ex.v = 2 }); r.define("a", (req, ex) => { ex.v = req("b").v + 1 }); let t = false; try { r.require("zzz") } catch { t = true }; assert(r.require("a").v === 3 && t, "deps")

takeaway.key: ESM: static imports, live bindings, one cached instance per module, tree-shakable. Use dynamic import() to split code.
mistakes: Expecting a module to run again on every import.
Mixing require and import in the same file.

dryRun.title: Three ways to get "only one"
dryRun.note: A singleton guarantees one shared instance (a logger, a config, an API client). In JavaScript a module export already is one. The cost: hidden shared state, which makes testing harder.

think.q:
class Config { static #i; static get() { return (Config.#i ??= new Config()) } }
console.log(Config.get() === Config.get())
why: The first call creates the instance; later calls return it.
think.exec:
class Config { static #i; static get() { return (Config.#i ??= new Config()) } }
console.log(Config.get() === Config.get())

think.q:
function makeLogger() { const lines = []; return { log: (s) => lines.push(s), count: () => lines.length } }
const a = makeLogger(), b = makeLogger()
a.log('x')
console.log(b.count())
why: A factory call gives a new instance each time. A singleton would share the lines.

think.q:
const counter = (() => { let n = 0; return { inc: () => ++n } })()
counter.inc()
const sameModuleImportedAgain = counter
console.log(sameModuleImportedAgain.inc())
why: Every importer gets the same object, so state is shared.
think.exec:
const counter = (() => { let n = 0; return { inc: () => ++n } })()
counter.inc()
const sameModuleImportedAgain = counter
console.log(sameModuleImportedAgain.inc())

think.q: What is the biggest downside of singletons?
opts: Hidden global state: tests and features affect each other through it
why: Prefer passing dependencies in where you can; keep singletons for truly app-wide things.

think.q: Which is a reasonable singleton?
opts: A list item in a todo app
One HTTP client with base URL and auth headers shared by the app
A user row from the database
why: Shared infrastructure, not data with many instances.

try.task: Write createSingleton(factory): returns { get(), reset() }. get creates the instance with factory on first use and returns the same one after that; reset forgets it (handy for tests).
examples: const s = createSingleton(() => ({ id: Math.random() })); s.get() === s.get()  // true
s.reset(); // next get() makes a new one
try.hint: Store the instance in a closure variable; use ??= in get.

checks.verify: const s = createSingleton(() => ({})); assert(s.get() === s.get() && typeof s.get() === "object", "same")

checks.t: lazy: factory runs on first get only
checks.verify: let n = 0; const s = createSingleton(() => (n++, {})); assert(n === 0, "eager"); s.get(); s.get(); assert(n === 1, "runs " + n)

checks.t: reset creates a new instance next time
checks.verify: const s = createSingleton(() => ({})); const a = s.get(); s.reset(); assert(s.get() !== a, "reset")

takeaway.key: A module export already is a singleton. Use one for shared infrastructure, and give tests a way to reset it.
mistakes: Singletons for things that should have many instances.
Tests leaking state into each other through a singleton.

dryRun.title: createShape(type, size)
rows: never uses new or knows the classes
dryRun.note: A factory is a function that creates objects for you, hiding which class or shape is used. Callers ask for "a circle", not for "new Circle". It also lets you return cached objects, mocks in tests, or different implementations per environment.

think.q:
const make = (type) => ({ circle: () => ({ sides: 0 }), square: () => ({ sides: 4 }) })[type]?.() ?? null
console.log(make('square').sides, make('blob'))
why: A lookup table of creators keeps the factory open for new types; unknown types return null here.
think.exec:
const make = (type) => ({ circle: () => ({ sides: 0 }), square: () => ({ sides: 4 }) })[type]?.() ?? null
console.log(make('square').sides, make('blob'))

think.q:
function createUser(name) { return { name, greet() { return 'hi ' + this.name } } }
const a = createUser('A'), b = createUser('B')
console.log(a.greet === b.greet)
why: Object-literal methods are created per object. Classes share methods on the prototype; for many objects that saves memory.

think.q:
function createCounter() { let n = 0; return { inc: () => ++n } }
const c = createCounter()
c.inc()
console.log(c.n, c.inc())
why: Factories with closures give real privacy: n is not a property.

think.q: Why might a team use createStorage() instead of new LocalStorageAdapter() everywhere?
opts: The factory can return a memory store in tests or SSR without changing callers
why: Callers depend on the shape, not on a concrete class.

think.q: When is a plain class usually better than a factory?
opts: When you create many instances and want shared prototype methods and instanceof
why: Classes share methods; factories with closures give privacy. Both are fine tools.

try.task: Write createNotifier(channel) returning an object with send(msg) that returns a string: "email: msg", "sms: msg" (cut to 20 chars), or "push: msg". Unknown channels throw. Callers must not need to know any class names.
try.hint: A lookup object from channel to a creator function.

checks.verify: let t = false; try { createNotifier("fax") } catch { t = true }; assert(t, "throw")

takeaway.key: A factory hides how objects are made: callers ask for a kind, the factory decides the implementation.
mistakes: Long if/else chains instead of a lookup table.
Per-object methods when you create thousands of objects.

dryRun.title: emitter.on("save", a); emitter.on("save", b); emitter.emit("save", doc)
dryRun.note: The observer (pub/sub) pattern lets parts of an app react to events without knowing each other. DOM events, Node's EventEmitter and state stores all use it. Always give subscribers a way to unsubscribe, or you leak.

think.q:
const t = new EventTarget()
const log = []
const h = (e) => log.push(e.type)
t.addEventListener('ping', h)
t.addEventListener('ping', h)
t.dispatchEvent(new Event('ping'))
console.log(log.length)
why: EventTarget ignores adding the exact same listener twice. Many hand-written emitters do not.
think.exec:
const t = new EventTarget()
const log = []
const h = (e) => log.push(e.type)
t.addEventListener('ping', h)
t.addEventListener('ping', h)
t.dispatchEvent(new Event('ping'))
console.log(log.length)

think.q:
const subs = new Set()
const subscribe = (fn) => (subs.add(fn), () => subs.delete(fn))
const unsub = subscribe((v) => console.log('got', v))
subs.forEach((f) => f(1))
unsub()
subs.forEach((f) => f(2))
why: Returning an unsubscribe function from subscribe is the cleanest API.

think.q:
const listeners = [() => { throw new Error('bad') }, () => console.log('second')]
for (const l of listeners) { try { l() } catch (e) { console.log('caught', e.message) } }
why: Without the try/catch one broken listener stops the others. Robust emitters isolate listener errors.
think.exec:
const listeners = [() => { throw new Error('bad') }, () => console.log('second')]
for (const l of listeners) { try { l() } catch (e) { console.log('caught', e.message) } }

think.q: In what order are listeners for one event called in Node's EventEmitter?
opts: In the order they were added
why: Synchronously, in registration order.

think.q: A component subscribes to a store on mount but never unsubscribes. What happens after it is removed?
opts: The store keeps the callback (and the component's closure) alive and keeps calling it
why: Unsubscribe in cleanup.

try.task: Implement class Emitter with on(name, fn) (returns an unsubscribe function), once(name, fn), and emit(name, ...args) returning how many listeners ran.
examples: const e = new Emitter(); const off = e.on("x", f); e.emit("x", 1)  // 1
e.once("y", g); e.emit("y"); e.emit("y")  // g ran once
try.hint: Store a Map from name to an array of listeners. once wraps fn in a function that removes itself first. Copy the array before looping in emit.

checks.verify: const e = new Emitter(); const got = []; e.on("x", (a, b) => got.push(a + b)); assert(e.emit("x", 1, 2) === 1 && got[0] === 3, "emit")
const e = new Emitter(); let n = 0; const off = e.on("x", () => n++); e.emit("x"); off(); e.emit("x"); assert(n === 1, "off")
const e = new Emitter(); let n = 0; e.once("y", () => n++); e.emit("y"); assert(e.emit("y") === 0 && n === 1, "once")

takeaway.key: Observer = subscribe, emit, unsubscribe. Return an unsubscribe function and call it on cleanup.
mistakes: Mutating the listener list while looping over it.
